strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and well-motivated limitation of reservoir computing: sequential processing and the O(Nh^2) memory footprint of dense reservoirs, by importing the diagonal complex linear recurrence of the LRU into the untrained-RC setting and parallelizing via associative scan.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad and well-organized for this area: memory tasks, forecasting (including real-world ETT datasets), UEA/UCR classification, sMNIST/psMNIST, comparisons against both classical RC baselines (ESN, deep ESN, SCR, Structured RC) and fully-trainable models (LSTM, Transformer, LRU, Mamba), with careful reporting of training time, energy, and CO2 emissions.

The efficiency claims are concretely supported: Fig. 2/4 and Tables 4-5 demonstrate logarithmic scaling in sequence length and order-of-magnitude reductions in training time/energy, and the OOM experiments for large reservoirs (Fig. 2 right) are a nice practical demonstration.
Hyperparameter sensitivity analysis (Fig. 6) and a comparison with other structured RC approaches (Table 9) are provided in the appendix, strengthening the credibility of the empirical claims.
The writing and figures are generally clear, and the paper is well-structured.
weaknesses: Originality is incremental: the core construction is essentially the LRU recurrence applied to an untrained reservoir with a fixed random mixing layer. The novelty lies in combining known components rather than a new architectural or algorithmic insight, and the paper could more clearly delineate what is new relative to (Orvieto et al., 2023) and linear SSMs.

The theoretical analysis is largely straightforward and partly over-claimed. Theorem 4.1 (ESP iff all |λi| < 1 for a linear diagonal system) is a trivial consequence of linearity. Proposition 4.2 asserts exact output equivalence via diagonalization, but the proof begins with 'Every square matrix is diagonalizable in the complex field, up to arbitrarily small perturbations' — this is not true for arbitrary matrices (defective matrices exist), and a perturbation argument would only yield approximate, not exact, equivalence as the proposition claims.

There is a mismatch between the theory and the practical model: universality (Corollary 4.3) requires an MLP readout over complex states, but in most experiments the readout is a linear ridge regressor (and the mixing layer is a random 1-D convolution, not a dense MLP), so the universality guarantees do not directly cover the configuration that is actually evaluated.

Some fairness concerns in the empirical comparison: ParalESN benefits from additional components (random mixing layers, deep stacking, concatenation of layer states) relative to the ESN baselines, and the accuracy gains over deep ESNs are modest and often not statistically significant per the critical difference plot, while headline gains over shallow ESNs are large; the contribution over ESN (deep) is less clear than the abstract suggests.

No dedicated limitations section; the paper does not discuss, e.g., sensitivity of performance to hyperparameter tuning (which Fig. 6 shows can be substantial for ρ, phases, and leaky rate), the 24-hour Bayesian search budget, or the potential fragility of the random convolutional mixing layer.
Reproducibility is weakened by the absence of a code release statement despite extensive benchmarking.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine practical limitation of Reservoir Computing (sequential processing and quadratic memory footprint of dense recurrent matrices) by combining diagonal complex linear recurrence (LRU-style) with the untrained-reservoir paradigm, enabling associative-scan parallelization. This is a sensible and timely direction for the RC community.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad for an RC paper: memory tasks, chaotic forecasting, real-world ETT forecasting, UEA/UCR classification, and sMNIST/psMNIST, with comparisons to LSTMs, Transformers, LRU, and Mamba, and reporting of training time, energy, and CO2 emissions alongside accuracy. Comparison to other structured RC approaches (SCR, Structured RC) in Appendix G is a good addition.

The computational complexity analysis (Appendix B, Table 5) is clear and the observation that associative scan is not practically applicable to dense or Hadamard-structured reservoirs is a useful, honest point that motivates the diagonal design.

The writing and figures (e.g., Fig. 1, Fig. 2) are generally clear, and the model selection protocol (Bayesian search, hyperparameter table, sensitivity analysis in Appendix G.1) is documented in reasonable detail.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is thin and partially flawed. Theorem 4.1 (ESP iff all |lambda_i| < 1) is an elementary contraction argument for a diagonal linear system. More importantly, the proof of Proposition 4.2 rests on the claim that 'every square matrix is diagonalizable in the complex field, up to arbitrarily small perturbations.' This is false as stated: perturbed matrices are only approximately equivalent, so the claimed exact equivalence ('for any given input, the two models produce the same output') does not follow. A density/approximation argument could likely repair the universality conclusion (Corollary 4.3), but the paper does not provide it, so the central expressivity claim is not rigorously established.

Limited originality. The architecture is essentially the LRU recurrence with random (untrained) weights plus a fixed random 1-D conv mixer; parallelization via associative scan is inherited from prior work (Martin & Cundy, 2018; Orvieto et al., 2023), and the universality of linear reservoirs with nonlinear readouts is already established (Grigoryeva & Ortega, 2018b; Gonon & Ortega, 2020). The delta over existing literature is modest.

Baseline fairness is a concern. ParalESN has roughly a dozen tunable hyperparameters (rho_min/max, theta_min/max, tau, mixer scalings, kernel size, number of layers, concat, etc.) tuned by a 24-hour Bayesian search, which may advantage it over baselines with fewer degrees of freedom. Additionally, for MNIST tasks the 'untrained' model actually includes a trained 2-layer MLP readout optimized with Adam, which blurs the RC-vs-fully-trained distinction the efficiency narrative relies on.

Several results are presented with inconsistencies that undermine confidence: the energy standard deviation exceeds the mean (0.04±0.1) for ParalESN on sMNIST (Table 4), and the ESN ETTm2 error has an implausibly large variance (9.9±7.3 in Table 2). These suggest measurement or reporting errors.

No code release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility given the large hyperparameter search space, and the paper contains no limitations section discussing, e.g., the 1-D convolutional mixer's restricted state mixing, the O(T N_h) state storage that still limits very long sequences despite scan parallelism, or applicability beyond the considered benchmark families.

Some central claims are stronger than the evidence: 'reducing computational costs and energy consumption by orders of magnitude' holds relative to some baselines, but Table 4 shows ~8-10x versus LRU/Mamba and the memory-scaling claim in Fig. 2 (right) is demonstrated only for one task and one hardware configuration.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: sequential processing and quadratic memory footprint of dense reservoirs are genuine limitations of RC, and the paper articulates the gap between classical RC and modern parallelizable sequence models (SSMs, LRU) convincingly.

The theoretical results are correct and appropriate for the setting: Theorem 4.1 gives a clean necessary-and-sufficient ESP condition for the diagonal linear recurrence (with a complete proof in Appendix C.1), and Proposition 4.2 connects ParalESN to arbitrary linear reservoirs via diagonalization, supporting the universality corollary via prior results (Grigoryeva & Ortega, 2018a;b).

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad for an RC paper: memory capacity, chaotic forecasting (Lorenz, Mackey-Glass), NARMA, real-world ETT forecasting, UEA/UCR classification, and sMNIST/psMNIST, with comparisons against ESN variants, SCR, Structured RC, LSTM, Transformer, LRU, and Mamba.

Computational efficiency is measured carefully and reported with useful detail (training time, energy, CO2 via CodeCarbon), and the complexity analysis in Appendix B (including why associative scan does not trivially apply to Structured RC) is a valuable addition.

Reasonable model-selection protocol (Bayesian search with matching budgets for RC and fully-trainable baselines, validation-based selection), hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, and statistical testing via critical difference plots.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core architecture is essentially an untrained LRU (diagonal complex linear recurrence with [rmin, rmax] eigenvalue parameterization) plus a frozen mixing layer and trainable readout. Both ingredients exist; the contribution is the combination and its RC framing, which reviewers may see as incremental. The paper does not clearly delineate what is new beyond applying known parallel-scan machinery to reservoirs.

The theoretical contribution is elementary: Theorem 4.1 for a diagonal linear system is nearly immediate, and Proposition 4.2 is a standard diagonalization argument (with the proof relying on 'every matrix is diagonalizable up to arbitrarily small perturbations', which deserves more care regarding how perturbations affect exact output equivalence). The universality result is largely inherited from prior work.

Mixed empirical results are somewhat downplayed: e.g., shallow ParalESN is worse than ESN on ctXOR5, FaultDetectionA (75.0 vs 71.3 for ESN but 86.0 for ESN-deep), and MG84, and differences between deep variants are often not statistically significant; headline claims of being 'more accurate and faster' rest partly on averaging and comparisons against the weaker shallow baseline.

The 'orders of magnitude' cost/energy savings versus fully-trainable models should be interpreted cautiously: comparisons are on relatively small benchmarks (sMNIST/psMNIST) with differing training regimes, and the ridge readout requires storing O(T Nh) hidden states, which is glossed over in the efficiency narrative for long sequences.

No explicit limitations section, and no clear statement about releasing the authors' own code (only baseline code links are given), which weakens reproducibility despite detailed hyperparameter listings.

Writing and polish issues remain: several grammatical errors ('an ParalESN', 'Fig. 3 compares ParalESN provides'), a nonstandard/loose formulation of the ESP in Eq. (3), and the boundary case |λ|=1 in Theorem 4.1's necessity argument is not fully addressed.
